Intermittent air mixing enhances dry anaerobic co-digestion of pig manure 
solid fraction and wheat straw: Methane performance and 
machine-learning-guided parameter optimization
Yue Zhao a,b, Yilin Wang a,b, Liangwei Deng a,b
, Wenguo Wang a,b, Xiaodong Pu a,b,  
Yongpan Xue c,d, Hongnan Yang a,b,*
a Biogas Institute of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China
b Key Laboratory of Development and Application of Rural Renewable Energy, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Chengdu 610041, PR China
c Hefei Wanhao Energy Equipment Co., Ltd, Hefei 230601, PR China
d Key Laboratory of Biomethane and Carbon Capture Technology, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Hefei 230601, PR China
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C  A B S T R A C T
• A 50:50 PMSF-straw ratio maximized 
synergy in dry co-digestion.
• Moderate air mixing raised VMPR by 
10.8 % at matched OLRs.
• Micro-aeration suppressed propionate 
and shifted VFAs toward acetate.
• SVR predicted VMPR accurately using 
TS, HRT, OLR, and air intensity.
• Feature fusion revealed indirect meta­
bolic drivers of air-mixing benefits.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Pig manure solid fraction
Wheat straw
Dry anaerobic digestion
Intermittent air mixing
Machine learning
A B S T R A C T
Dry anaerobic co-digestion of pig manure solid fraction (PMSF) and wheat straw was optimized using 
biochemical methane potential assays, semi-continuous full-factorial operation, microbial profiling, and machine 
learning. The strongest substrate synergy occurred at a 50:50 total solids (TS)-based PMSF-to-straw ratio. Under 
matched organic loading rates (OLRs), intermittent air mixing at 33.3 mL L−1 min−1, applied once daily for 1 
min, improved volumetric methane production rate by an average of 10.8 %, reduced propionate accumulation, 
and shifted volatile fatty acids toward acetate, whereas excessive air input weakened performance. Support 
vector regression using TS, hydraulic retention time, OLR, and air-mixing intensity showed the best cross- 
validated performance (R2 = 0.912; root mean square error = 0.101 L L−1 d−1). Feature analysis associated 
methane production primarily with OLR, acetate-related metabolic state, and selected microbial genera; the 
microbial model was interpreted as exploratory because of its small sample size. These findings define an 
operation window for data-driven optimization of high-solids agricultural-waste digestion.

1. Introduction
The rapid development of intensive livestock and poultry farming 
industry has led to a massive localized concentration of swine waste­
water (Deng et al., 2023). Solid–liquid separation is widely used as a 
pretreatment because it reduces the organic load entering subsequent 
units and improves manure utilization efficiency (Liao et al., 2025; 
Osabutey et al., 2023). The retained solid product, pig manure solid 
fraction (PMSF), is usually enriched in organic matter relative to whole 
manure and may contain higher total or organic nitrogen, depending on 
the separation process, while readily soluble organics preferentially 
remain in the liquid phase (Pantelopoulos & Aronsson, 2021; Vergote 
et al., 2020). These compositional shifts can slow hydrolysis, weaken 
substrate conversion, and increase the risks of ammonia inhibition and 
alkalinity-buffer imbalance during mono-anaerobic digestion. Dry co- 
digestion of PMSF with carbon-rich straw is therefore a promising 
strategy to improve the C/N ratio, enhance reactor volumetric treatment 
capacity, and reduce digestate liquor generation. However, previous 
research has mainly addressed liquid swine wastewater or unseparated 
pig manure co-digested with straw (Liu & Pan, 2023; Rajagopal et al., 
2022; Wang et al., 2021). The digestion performance, optimal substrate 
ratio, synergistic degradation mechanisms, and parameter adaptation 
boundaries of PMSF–straw systems under dry anaerobic conditions 
remain insufficiently clarified.
Dry anaerobic digestion systems, typically operated at a feed total 
solids (TS) content of 20–40 %, are often constrained by high substrate 
viscosity, localized acidification, and the slow hydrolysis of macromo­
lecular organic matter (e.g., lignocellulose), which together limit mass 
transfer and methanogenic efficiency. These limitations are more pro­
nounced at elevated total solids, where insufficient contact among 
substrates, enzymes, and microorganisms can delay acidogenesis and 
methanogenesis. Recently, controlled oxygen introduction through 
intermittent air mixing or micro-aeration has received increasing 
attention as a biochemical enhancement strategy, with reported 
biomethane-yield improvements of 13 %–77 % (Chuenchart et al., 2025; 
Mahdy et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2019). Intermittent air mixing sup­
plies transient electron acceptors for facultative anaerobic hydrolytic 
bacteria and improves interfacial mass transfer through biochemical 
stimulation and localized physical perturbation (Li et al., 2023; Song 
et al., 2026; Yang & Deng, 2020). This micro-oxygen strategy may thus 
help overcome the hydrolysis bottleneck of high-solid substrates in dry 
anaerobic digestion.
Nevertheless, process regulation remains difficult because substrate 
concentration, hydraulic retention time (HRT), organic loading rate 
(OLR), and aeration intensity interact in complex, nonlinear ways dur­
ing dry anaerobic digestion (Rocamora et al., 2020). Traditional single- 
factor experiments cannot fully reveal these synergistic effects, while 
classical kinetic models such as the Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 
(ADM1) often require challenging parameter calibration and show 
limited predictive accuracy in high-solid systems (Pastor-Poquet et al., 
2018). Data-driven machine learning (ML) has therefore become a 
useful tool in anaerobic digestion modeling (Long et al., 2025). ML 
models can capture nonlinear relationships in dynamic fermentation 
environments and often outperform purely mechanistic approaches in 
prediction tasks (Park et al., 2021). Recent studies further show that 
integrating high-throughput microbiome data with macroscopic oper­
ating parameters and physicochemical state indicators can improve 
methanogenic prediction accuracy and identify key operational vari­
ables and microbial markers through feature-importance analysis (Dang 
et al., 2025; Long et al., 2021).
Accordingly, this study examined intermittently air-mixed dry co- 
digestion of PMSF and straw using biochemical methane potential as­
says, semi-continuous experiments, physicochemical analyses, degra­
dation kinetics, and 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) amplicon sequencing. 
The objectives were to determine the optimal total-solids ratio and 
synergistic methane effect; evaluate, through a complete three-factor, 
three-level combination matrix, the combined effects of feed total 
solids, HRT, OLR, and trace air input on volumetric methane production 
and metabolic stability; and build an ML model that fuses operational, 
physicochemical, and microbial features. Model evaluation and feature- 
importance analysis were used to quantify parameter contributions and 
interactions, identify operational constraints, and support interpretation 
of the tested operating window for engineering application of high-solid 
air-mixed fermentation for agricultural wastes.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Pig manure solid fraction (PMSF) was collected from the solid phase 
retained after hydraulic screen solid–liquid separation of wastewater at 
a fattening-pig farm in Chengdu, Sichuan Province, China, and was 
stored frozen at −20 ◦C. Wheat straw was obtained from an agricultural- 
product processing facility in Lianyungang, Jiangsu Province, China, 
crushed, and sieved to 0.5 −1.0 cm. The inoculum was collected from a 
mesophilic swine-wastewater digester and acclimated at 55 ◦C until 
endogenous biogas production stabilized. Basic substrate and inoculum 
characteristics are provided in Table S1.
2.2. Experimental design
2.2.1. Optimization of the PMSF-to-straw mixing ratio
Batch biochemical methane potential (BMP) tests were used to 
evaluate PMSF-straw synergy at TS-based ratios of 100:0, 75:25, 50:50, 
25:75, and 0:100 (detailed experimental design in Table S2). Each 500 
mL fermentation bottle contained 34.5 g TS of substrate and 25.5 g TS 
inoculum sludge in a total working mass of 300 g. All treatments and 
inoculum blanks were conducted in triplicate. After nitrogen purging, 
the bottles were incubated at 55 ◦C for 45 d. Daily biogas production was 
measured by water displacement using a water-filled gas collector 
connected via latex tubing. Methane production was calculated from the 
measured biogas volume and methane fraction. The mean methane 
production of the inoculum blanks was subtracted from each treatment, 
and cumulative methane production was obtained by summing the 
blank-corrected values. The expected cumulative methane production of 
the mixed substrates was calculated using TS-mass-fraction weighting of 
the two mono-substrates, as described in Equation (1): 
E = MPMSF • fPMSF + Mstraw • fstraw
(1) 
where MPMSF and Mstraw are the cumulative methane production values 
of the corresponding mono-digestion controls, and fPMSF and fstraw are 
their VS fractions in the mixture. The synergistic enhancement rate was 
calculated as ΔY = (A −E)/E × 100%, where A and E represent actual 
and expected cumulative methane production, respectively. When ΔY >
0, it indicates a positive synergistic effect.
2.2.2. Optimization of dry anaerobic digestion process parameters
After the 50:50 TS-based PMSF-to-straw ratio was selected, a com­
plete three-factor, three-level combination matrix was used to evaluate 
feed TS (Feed TS: 20 %, 25 %, and 30 %), hydraulic retention time (HRT: 
25 d, 35 d, and 45 d), and intermittent air mixing intensity (0, 33.3, and 
66.7 mL L−1 min−1), producing 27 operating conditions and calculated 
OLRs of 4.4–12.0 g TS L−1 d−1 (corresponding to VS-based OLRs of g VS 
L−1 d−1). Each operated in triplicate. Feed-TS levels were selected to 
span the operational dry-digestion range used in this study; HRTs were 
selected to cover a practical retention-time gradient for thermophilic 
high-solids digestion; and the air levels bracketed moderate and higher 
intensities reported for high-solids air-mixing systems (Li et al., 2023; 
Song et al., 2026; Yang & Deng, 2020). Because OLR was calculated from 
feed TS and HRT, it was not treated as an independent experimental 
factor.

The experiment was conducted using 0.5 L glass digesters with a 
working volume of 0.3 L. Each digester was equipped with an air inlet 
connected to an aeration head positioned near the reactor bottom, a 
biogas outlet connected to an aluminum gas bag, and an N2 inlet for 
headspace flushing. All digesters were manually shaken two to three 
times daily.
Because the high-solids substrate could not be transferred reliably 
through a syringe port, feeding and discharging were conducted gravi­
metrically once daily by briefly opening the reactor. A wet mass corre­
sponding to 1/HRT of the reactor contents was removed and replaced 
with an equal wet mass of fresh feed. The reactor was then resealed and 
flushed with N2 for 1 min before application of the prescribed air pulse. 
Detailed operating conditions for the semi-continuous parameter opti­
mization experiment are provided in Table S3.
The 0 mL L−1 min−1 treatment served as the no air-mixing control. 
For the 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 treatment, air was introduced once per day at 
10 mL min−1 for 1 min. For the 66.7 mL L−1 min−1 treatment, air was 
introduced once per day at 20 mL min−1 for 1 min. Daily biogas was 
collected in aluminum gas bags and quantified using a gas-tight syringe. 
Daily methane volume was calculated as collected biogas volume 
multiplied by the methane fraction, and volumetric methane production 
rate (VMPR) was obtained by dividing daily methane volume by the 
0.30 L working volume. The reactors were operated for 38–45 d, cor­
responding to approximately 1.0–1.5 HRTs depending on the treatment. 
Methane production stabilization was defined as less than 10 % varia­
tion in VMPR over 20 consecutive days.
2.3. Physicochemical analysis and microbial community analysis
Biogas composition was measured using a gas chromatograph 
equipped with a thermal conductivity detector. TS, Volatile solid (VS), 
and pH were determined according to Standard Methods (APHA, 2012). 
NH4
+-N was determined colorimetrically using Nessler reagent. Total 
carbon and total nitrogen contents were determined using an elemental 
analyzer (UNICUBE, Elementar, Germany). Total chemical oxygen de­
mand (TCOD) and soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) were 
determined using the potassium dichromate method. For SCOD analysis, 
samples were filtered through a 0.45 μm membrane before measure­
ment, whereas unfiltered samples were used for TCOD determination. 
Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) were quantified by gas chromatograph (GC- 
2030, Shimadzu, Japan) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) 
(column temperature 180 ◦C, injector 200 ◦C, detector 230 ◦C) after 
centrifugation (10000 rpm for 10 min), filtration (0.22 μm), and acidi­
fication with 3 % (w/w) formic acid. Free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was 
estimated from measured ammoniacal nitrogen and pH at 55 ◦C using 
the NH4
+/NH3 equilibrium.
After stable semi-continuous operation, representative digestate 
samples covering low, medium, and high OLRs and all three air-mixing 
intensities were collected for 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing 
(Table S3). Sludge samples were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen 
and stored at −80 ◦C. Total DNA was extracted using a soil/feces 
genomic DNA extraction kit and assessed by electrophoresis and Qubit 
quantification. The bacterial V3–V4 region was amplified using primers 
341F(5′-CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG-3′) and 805R (5′-GACTACHVGGG­
TATCTAATCC-3′). Archaeal amplicons were obtained by nested PCR 
using 
340F 
(5′-CCCTAYGGGGYGCASCAG-3′) 
and 
1000R 
(5′- 
GGCCATGCACYWCYTCTC-3′) in the first round, followed by 349F (5′- 
GYGCASCAGKCGMGAAW-3′) and 806R (5′-GGACTACVSGGGTATC­
TAAT-3′) in the second round. Purified amplicon libraries were 
sequenced on an Illumina high-throughput paired-end sequencing 
platform. Raw reads were denoised, chimera-filtered, taxonomically 
annotated, and used to analyze community succession. The raw 
sequence data were deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology 
Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession 
number PRJNA1497691.
2.4. Machine-learning model construction and feature analysis
Data-driven modeling of VMPR was conducted in Python using 
scikit-learn and XGBoost packages. Because high-solids anaerobic 
digestion involves nonlinear coupling among operating conditions, 
metabolic intermediates, and microbial succession, a staged feature- 
fusion strategy was used to balance prediction accuracy and interpret­
ability. Three input matrices were constructed at the operating- 
condition level: Macro-27 (n = 27), including feed TS, HRT, OLR, and 
air mixing intensity; Macro-physicochemical-27 (n = 27), which further 
included NH4
+-N, FAN, total VFAs, acetate, propionate, butyrate, and VS 
removal; and Full-microbe-9 (n = 9), which combined these variables 
with selected microbial genera. For Full-microbe-9, SelectKBest with the 
univariate F-test was incorporated into the modeling pipeline to retain 
the five features most strongly associated with VMPR.
Random forest regression (RFR), extreme gradient boosting 
(XGBoost), and support vector regression (SVR) were evaluated as 
nonlinear regression models. RFR was used for nonlinear interaction 
analysis and feature-importance extraction, XGBoost as a regularized 
boosting benchmark, and SVR for kernel-based prediction in low- 
dimensional datasets (Chen & Guestrin, 2016). Fixed hyperparameter 
settings were used for all models without automated grid or randomized 
search. Model complexity was constrained using shallow tree depths and 
regularization settings, particularly for the small microbial dataset. The 
main settings were 80 trees with maximum depths of 4 and 2 for RFR in 
the 27- and 9-sample datasets, respectively; radial basis function (RBF)- 
SVR with C values of 10 and 5, respectively; and XGBoost with 
maximum depths of 2 and 1 and a learning rate of 0.05, respectively.
Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) was applied without a 
separate hold-out test set. For the 27-sample datasets, each fold used 26 
samples for training and one for validation; for Full-microbe-9, each fold 
used eight samples for training and one for validation. Each sample 
served once as the validation sample, and model performance was 
calculated from the pooled out-of-fold predictions using coefficient of 
determination (R2), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute 
error (MAE) (Long et al., 2021). For Full-microbe-9, feature selection 
was performed within the modeling pipeline in each LOOCV fold. The 
models were used to identify influential variables and favorable 
parameter combinations within the investigated experimental range. 
Random-forest impurity-based feature importance was interpreted as a 
model-based contribution indicator rather than causal evidence, 
particularly for correlated predictors. The modeling outputs were jointly 
interpreted with acetate/propionate ratio and VS removal to infer pro­
cess interactions.
2.5. Statistical analysis
Quantitative data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) 
from three biological replicates unless otherwise stated. For BMP data, 
one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s honestly 
significant difference test was used for pairwise comparisons. Within 
each air-mixing intensity, semi-continuous VMPR data were evaluated 
by one-way ANOVA across OLR conditions and by two-way ANOVA for 
feed TS, HRT, and their interaction. Microbial community differences 
were tested by two-way permutational multivariate analysis of variance 
(PERMANOVA) on Bray–Curtis dissimilarities with 9,999 permutations 
for air mixing, OLR, and their interaction. Spearman rank correlation 
was used for genus–VMPR associations. Statistical significance was set at 
p < 0.05.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Effects of substrate ratio on methane production and synergistic 
response
The BMP tests showed that co-digestion of PMSF and wheat straw

produced positive synergistic effects across all mixed treatments 
(Table 1). Among the co-digestion treatments, the 75:25 treatment 
achieved the highest cumulative methane production (6986 mL CH4) 
and methane yield (243 mL CH4 g−1 TS), which were not significantly 
different from those obtained from PMSF mono-digestion (p > 0.05). 
When the straw proportion exceeded 25 %, cumulative methane pro­
duction and methane yield declined, likely due to the increasing 
contribution of recalcitrant lignocellulosic material. In terms of syner­
gistic enhancement, however, the 50:50 ratio showed the strongest 
positive response (15.1 %). This suggests effective substrate comple­
mentarity: PMSF may have improved nutrient balance, while the rigid 
straw structure could increase bed porosity and mass transfer under 
high-solids conditions (Hanum et al., 2022; Ning et al., 2019). Consid­
ering both synergistic methane production and the need for large-scale 
straw valorization, the 50:50 TS-based ratio was selected for subse­
quent process optimization.
3.2. Interactive effects of OLR and intermittent air mixing on methane 
performance
OLR and HRT are key parameters determining the treatment in­
tensity of dry anaerobic digestion. Across the tested operating condi­
tions, the volumetric methane production rate (VMPR) generally 
increased with OLR (see Table 2); however, when the OLR exceeded 6.7 
g VS L−1 d−1 and the HRT was shortened to 25 d, specific methane yield 
(SMY) decreased markedly, reaching a minimum of 0.178 L CH4 g−1 VS. 
This trade-off suggests that the high loading increased the amount of 
convertible organic matter per reactor volume, but the shortened 
retention time and high-solids matrix limited hydrolysis and down­
stream conversion, allowing part of the particulate substrate to leave the 
reactor before complete bioconversion (Zhang et al., 2023).
Intermittent air mixing at a mixing intensity of 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 
consistently improved VMPR. In all nine matched OLR comparisons, this 
treatment increased VMPR relative to the no air-mixing control, with an 
average increase of 10.8 % and a range of 2.8–18.0 %. The maximum 
VMPR of 2.12 L CH4 L−1 d−1 occurred at 30 % feed TS, 25 d HRT, and 
10.1 g VS L−1 d−1 OLR. These results indicate that moderate air mixing 
promoted hydrolytic conversion (Li et al., 2023). In addition, the 
methane content remained relatively stable at 61–67 % following air 
addition (Fig. S1). This response may be associated with rapid oxygen 
consumption by facultative anaerobes, maintenance of anaerobic micro 
−
niches for methanogens (Fu et al., 2023), and possible CO2 con­
sumption through hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis or homoaceto­
genesis (Chuenchart et al., 2025).
When the air-mixing intensity was increased to 66.7 mL L−1 min−1, 
the enhancement weakened. Compared with the 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 
treatment, the 66.7 mL L−1 min−1 treatment showed lower VMPR in all 
matched comparisons, indicating that air mixing has an appropriate 
operating window. Excess oxygen may increase the local redox potential 
and intensify competition by facultative microorganisms for readily 
degradable substrates, thereby decreasing the efficiency of strictly 
anaerobic methanogenesis (Morais et al., 2024). Under the conditions 
tested here, 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 was the most suitable intermittent air- 
mixing intensity.
3.3. Effects of OLR-air mixing interaction on intermediate metabolism 
and process stability
3.3.1. Solid degradation and ammonium variation
VS removal reflects the degree of organic substrate degradation, 
whereas NH4
+-N concentration indicates the mineralization of nitroge­
nous organics (Proch´azka et al., 2012). As shown in Fig. 1(a), VS 
removal fluctuated with OLR rather than decreasing monotonically, 
indicating that organic-matter removal was influenced by feedstock 
characteristics and operational stage rather than by OLR alone (Gao 
et al., 2023). At matched OLRs, intermittent air mixing at 33.3 mL L−1 
min−1 generally increased VS removal, indicating enhanced solids 
degradation under dry digestion conditions. This response is consistent 
with previous reports that air mixing can enhance hydrolysis and the 
solubilization of particulate organics in high-solids AD systems (Fu et al., 
2023; Li et al., 2023).
Meanwhile, NH4
+-N in the moderate-air group remained relatively 
high (1521–1918 mg L−1) across increasing OLRs, while the corre­
sponding free ammonia nitrogen (FAN) was ranged from174 to 224 mg 
NH3-N L−1 (Fig. 1(b)). The FAN concentrations observed here were 
lower than levels associated with pronounced inhibition in several 
thermophilic digestion systems (approximately 560–700 mg NH3-N L−1) 
(Sung & Liu, 2003). Thus, severe FAN inhibition was not evident in the 
moderate-air treatment within the tested OLR range. Together with 
limited VFA accumulation, the methane-production response indicated 
no pronounced FAN-related deterioration during the observation 
period.
3.3.2. VFA accumulation and component transformation
VFA concentration and composition are key diagnostic indicators of 
biochemical balance under loading stress because VFA accumulation, 
especially a shift toward propionate dominance, typically reflects an 
imbalance between acidogenesis/acetogenesis and methanogenesis 
(Maurus et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022). As shown in Fig. 1(c), total VFA 
concentrations showed a non-monotonic response to OLR and were 
strongly affected by air mixing intensity. The high-air treatment (66.7 
mL L−1 min−1) produced relatively high total VFA concentrations at 
most OLRs, reaching about 1000 mg L−1 at OLR 4.8 g VS L−1 d−1. In the 
no-air control, marked VFA accumulation occurred mainly at OLRs 5.6 
and 7.2 g VS L−1 d−1. The no-air control was consistently propionate- 
rich, with propionate accounting for approximately 50–72 % of total 
VFAs. The 66.7 mL L−1 min−1 treatment was also propionate-dominated 
at most OLRs, although acetate slightly exceeded propionate at OLRs 
4.7–4.8 g VS L−1 d−1.
By contrast, the 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 air-mixing treatment maintained 
total VFA concentrations at a moderate level of approximately 490–820 
mg L−1 across the loading gradient. Although this treatment was not 
consistently the lowest among all treatments, it generally showed lower 
VFA accumulation than the 66.7 mL L−1 min−1 treatment and exhibited 
a less propionate-dominated acid spectrum. Under 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 
air mixing, acetate accounted for approximately 40–46 % of total VFAs, 
while propionate accounted for approximately 37–44 %, indicating a 
more balanced distribution between acetate and propionate and a 
relative shift toward an acetate-enriched VFA profile.
From a biochemical thermodynamic perspective, the high physical 
viscosity of the dry digestion matrix increased gas–liquid transfer 
resistance and hindered the local removal of reduced intermediates and 
electron carriers, particularly H2/formate, by hydrogenotrophic part­
ners (Gao et al., 2023; Westerholm et al., 2022). As the feed load 
increased, enhanced acidification and elevated local H2/formate

pressure may make syntrophic propionate oxidation to acetate ther­
modynamically less favorable, thereby contributing to propionate 
retention (Jin & Lu, 2023; Wu et al., 2022).
Trace oxygen introduced by moderate air mixing can act as a high- 
potential electron acceptor and may be rapidly consumed by faculta­
tive bacteria, thereby maintaining anaerobic micro-niches for obligate 
anaerobes while modifying local redox conditions (Fu et al., 2023; 
Morais et al., 2024). This process could reduce excess reducing equiv­
alents and help maintain lower local H2/formate pressure under loading 
stress, potentially relieving the thermodynamic constraint on propionate 
degradation and promoting the conversion of intermediates toward 
acetate (Morais et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2019).
Therefore, the improvement in VMPR observed in Section 3.2 is 
mechanistically consistent with the VFA data. Moderate air mixing was 
associated with reduced propionate dominance and a relatively more 
acetate-enriched VFA pool, suggesting that appropriate air-mixing in­
tensity may help alleviate intermediate accumulation and improve the 
availability of methanogenic substrates. This shift in VFA composition 
may partly explain the enhanced methane production performance 
observed under the 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 air-mixing treatment.
3.4. Effects of OLR-air mixing interaction on microbial community 
succession
3.4.1. Bacterial community response
16S rRNA amplicon sequencing revealed shifts in bacterial commu­
nity composition across the OLR and air-mixing treatments (Fig. 2 (a, 
b)). Two-way PERMANOVA showed significant effects of air mixing, 
OLR, and their interaction at both the phylum and genus levels (all p <
0.001). At the phylum level, Bacillota (Firmicutes) and Pseudomonadota 
(Proteobacteria) were dominant across all operating conditions. Under 
the no air mixing condition (A0), the relative-abundance profiles 
appeared comparatively similar across load levels, and norank_MBA03 
was the most abundant genus-level lineage. This uncultured Bacillota 
lineage has previously been associated with syntrophic acetate oxidation 
in consortia containing hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Puchol-Royo 
et al., 2025).
After the introduction of intermittent air mixing at 33.3 mL L−1 
min−1, the bacterial community showed stronger load-dependent dif­
ferentiation. Under the boundary-load condition of 30 % TS and 25 
d HRT, Pseudomonas, Psychrobacter, and Ruminiclostridium were rela­
tively enriched. The enrichment of Pseudomonas and Psychrobacter may 
reflect the presence of facultative or aerotolerant populations capable of 
occupying micro-oxic niches and contributing to oxygen consumption, 
whereas the enrichment of Ruminiclostridium may be consistent with 
greater cellulolytic potential (Costa et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2023). Thus, 
these taxonomic shifts suggest enhanced oxygen-scavenging and hy­
drolytic potential under moderate air input and high OLR.
3.4.2. Archaeal community response
The archaeal taxonomic profiles varied significantly among the OLR 
and air mixing treatments (Fig. 2 (c, d)). At the phylum level, two-way 
PERMANOVA showed significant effects of air mixing (p < 0.001), OLR 
(p = 0.002), and their interaction (p < 0.001). Significant effects were 
also detected at the genus level for air mixing (p < 0.001), OLR (p <
0.001), and their interaction (p = 0.002). Methanosarcina, a genus con­
taining methanogens with broad substrate-utilization capabilities, 
dominated all treatments (Carr & Buan, 2022). In the no air-mixing 
group, the archaeal community-maintained coexistence of hydro­
genotrophic methanogens (approximately 41 %) and acetoclastic 
methanogens across feed concentrations and HRTs.
Under moderate air mixing condition (33.3 mL L−1 min−1), the 
archaeal community exhibited a pronounced directional shift with 
increasing OLR. The relative abundance of Methanosarcina increased 
sharply and exceeded 89 % under the highest-load condition, whereas 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens declined. Together with the higher ac­
etate/propionate ratio observed under moderate air mixing condition, 
this compositional shift is consistent with a possible increase in the 
contribution of acetoclastic methanogenesis. Given the metabolic 
versatility of Methanosarcina, this enrichment is therefore best inter­
preted as ecological evidence supporting a greater acetoclastic contri­
bution rather than as an exclusive indication of a single methanogenic 
route. Members of Methanosarcina have been reported to be competitive 
under acetate-rich, high-load, and fluctuating conditions (Carr & Buan, 
2022; Ziganshin et al., 2016), a while some strains can tolerate transient 
oxygen exposure through antioxidant systems, biofilm formation, or 
protection within syntrophic consortia (Fu et al., 2023; Jasso-Ch´avez 
et al., 2015). The relatively high NH4
+-N level may have further 
contributed to this selective pressure. Accordingly, the strong enrich­
ment of Methanosarcina suggests selective persistence under moderate

3.5. Machine-learning prediction, optimization, and mechanism 
interpretation
3.5.1. Model performance using different input feature combinations
Stable anaerobic digestion performance and methane production 
result from nonlinear coupling among operating conditions, intermedi­
ate metabolites, and microbial community structure. Therefore, the 
purpose of the staged ML analysis was not only to maximize R2 but also 
to connect the external controls tested in Section 3.2 with the metabolic 
and microbial evidence presented in Sections 3.3 and 3.4. In the Macro- 
27 matrix containing only feed TS, HRT, OLR, and air mixing, SVR 
showed the best predictive performance (R2 = 0.912; RMSE = 0.101 L 
L−1 d−1) (Fig. 3(a, b)). This result is reasonable because OLR integrates 
the combined effects of feed TS and HRT and, as shown experimentally, 
largely determines the upper boundary of VMPR. Kernel-based SVR can 
capture this nonlinear operating boundary even with a limited number 
of external variables (Long et al., 2021). However, this performance 
should be interpreted as interpolation within the tested factorial domain 
rather than proof of extrapolative predictability outside the present TS- 
HRT-air-dose range.
When the input was expanded to the Macro-physicochemical-27 
matrix, XGBoost provided the best LOOCV predictive performance 
(R2 = 0.898; RMSE = 0.109 L L−1 d−1) (Fig. 3(a, b)). The inclusion of 
intermediate physicochemical variables resulted in slightly lower 
overall predictive performance than that of Macro-27 while incorpo­
rating information on the internal biochemical state of the reactor. The 
similar performance of XGBoost and RFR indicates that ensemble-tree 
models effectively captured the nonlinear relationships among oper­
ating conditions and physicochemical responses. This staged modeling 
strategy complemented the macroscopic model by linking external 
operating controls with the internal metabolic state associated with air- 
mixing responses.
For the Full-microbe-9 matrix, dimensionality reduction was essen­
tial because only nine sequencing samples were available. SelectKBest 
was incorporated into the modeling pipeline to retain five features from 
the fused operating, physicochemical, and microbial feature set. 
RFR_SelectK5 showed the best LOOCV performance (R2 = 0.837; RMSE 
= 0.188 L L−1 d−1), compared with XGBoost_SelectK5 (R2 = 0.575; 
RMSE = 0.303 L L−1 d−1) and SVR_SelectK5 (R2 = 0.405; RMSE = 0.359 
L L−1 d−1) (Fig. 3(a, b)). These results are consistent with recent 
anaerobic-digestion modeling studies showing that microbial profiles 
can improve mechanistic resolution but may also increase variance 
when the number of samples is small relative to the number of predictors 
(Dang et al., 2025; Long et al., 2021). Therefore, the microbial model 
was used primarily to identify process-relevant biological markers and 
their associations with operating parameters within the investigated 
experimental range.
3.5.2. Feature contribution and interpretation of the air-mixing effect
Feature importance extracted from the RFR model quantified the 
model-based contributions of individual variables to VMPR. In the 
Macro-27 matrix, OLR was the dominant determinant of VMPR, with an 
importance of 0.950 (Fig. 3(c)). This agrees with the experimental trend 
in Section 3.2 that increasing the amount of organic substrate entering 
the reactor raised VMPR.
After core process variables were added in the Macro-physicochemical- 
27 matrix, the distribution of variable importance changed substantially. 
OLR remained the most important variable (0.916), but acetate became the 
most influential physicochemical variable (0.0322), followed by VS 
removal (0.0077), total VFAs (0.0068), propionate (0.0066), butyrate 
(0.0064), FAN (0.0058), and NH4
+-N (0.0047) (Fig. 3(d)). The direct 
importance of air mixing decreased from 0.0184 in Macro-27 to 0.0017 
after the physicochemical variables were incorporated. This importance

vant; instead, it indicates a mediation pathway. The paired experiments 
showed that air mixing at 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 increased VS removal, sup­
pressed propionate accumulation, and promoted acetate formation, 
whereas air mixing at 66.7 mL L−1 min−1 weakened these benefits. Once 
acetate, propionate, total VFAs, FAN, NH4
+-N, and VS removal were 
included in the model, the contribution associated with air mixing was 
redistributed toward these downstream process-state variables. Because 
random-forest importance can be redistributed among correlated pre­
dictors, the feature ranking was interpreted together with the paired OLR- 
air mixing comparisons and microbial data rather than as a standalone 
causal test (Strobl et al., 2008).
The microbial feature-fusion model further supported this indirect- 
effect interpretation. The five features retained by the fitted RFR_Se­
lectK5 model were HRT (importance = 0.296), feed TS (0.279), OLR 
(0.174), Methanobacterium (0.142), and Ureibacillus (0.109) (Fig. 3(e)). 
Methanobacterium and Ureibacillus also showed positive Spearman as­
sociations with VMPR (ρ = 0.65 and 0.67, respectively) (Fig. 3(f)). The 
selection of Methanobacterium indicates that performance remained 
sensitive to hydrogenotrophic methanogenic capacity even though 
Methanosarcina became dominant under the highest-load, moderate air- 
mixing condition. This does not contradict the rise of acetoclastic 
Methanosarcina described in Section 3.4.2; rather, it suggests that high 
VMPR remained associated with residual hydrogenotrophic capacity. 
Such capacity may support hydrogen/formate transfer relevant to pro­
pionate oxidation, while acetate provides substrate for Methanosarcina 
methanogenesis (Jin & Lu, 2023; Westerholm et al., 2022). Taken 
together, the ML and experimental results associate moderate air mixing 
with changes in taxa potentially related to oxygen scavenging or hy­
drolysis, lower propionate dominance and an acetate-enriched VFA 
profile, and a methanogenic community compatible with conversion of 
these intermediates.
3.5.3. Process-parameter optimization based on model interpretation
Integrating the complete 27-condition matrix with staged machine- 
learning interpretation showed that the favorable operating window 
could not be identified by maximizing any single variable. A high OLR 
increased VMPR but reduced SMY under no-air-mixing operation; 
moderate air input improved hydrolysis and VFA conversion; and 
excessive air input weakened methanogenic efficiency. Under the con­
ditions tested, the best observed semi-continuous combination was a 
50:50 TS-based PMSF-to-wheat straw ratio, 30 % feed TS, 25 d HRT, a TS 
loading rate of 12.0 g TS L−1 d−1 (corresponding to an OLR of 10.1 g VS 
L−1 d−1), and 33.3 mL L−1 min−1 intermittent air input.
Within this operating window, moderate air mixing was associated 
with higher VS removal, lower propionate dominance, and a more 
acetate-oriented VFA profile, while FAN remained below levels 
commonly associated with pronounced inhibition. The highest VMPR 
was 2.118 L CH4 L−1 d−1, and methane production met the predefined 
stabilization criterion during the observation period. The ML analysis 
was therefore used as an explanatory decision-support tool within the 
tested domain, with acetate/propionate distribution, total VFAs, NH4

procedures were performed on live animals, and the study did not 
involve human participants, human data, or human biological materials.
